entry.title: What's in a name?
entry.content:
Written as a part of writing prompt given at https://blr.indiewebclub.org/prompts/#october-19-2026

What’s the story behind your domain name? (Or your government name, or your online handle.)

So I own this domain name, hemish.net, and it’s surprisingly good that I have it: a regular-sounding ".net" domain name, and I pay pretty cheap for it. There is a reason it’s a single name domain name, which is my first name, my legal first name (which would get clearer later in this blog). Some people do include last names in their domain names, but I don’t have one.

My first name is Hemish. The story I have been told how this name got into the picture, is that Hemish Marshall is a former cricketer from New Zealand. My father, was a good player in his time as a young person. So, for the love of cricket, he named me "Hemish".

Even my sister, who is Chelsi, has gotten an English name like me. Coming from the background my father isfrom, it was very forward of my father to give his children English names in such a setting, which is very great, I would say.

Mononym

From my childhood, my father has put only my first name in all of my legal documents, starting from the birth certificate and then the later aadhar card. So when I grew up, naturally I only had my first name in everything, and wherever I need to put my name, I put it as-it-is. Even my passport has just my first name and the last name field is just blank.

Because of this, I do run into various issues a lot of times. Some of the websites don’t accept an empty last name, and I have to do a lot of workarounds. Sometimes, I put empty unicode characters there. Sometimes, I put a dot or underscore there. Sometimes, I duplicate my first name into the last name. But there is not a single standard which works everywhere, so I have to keep fiddling around with all of these options. So yeah, that’s how life is.

People say that I am going to have issues if I visit a foreign country. Yes, I would, but isn’t that my purpose, like I have to circumvent around these issues? So yeah, I prefer to stay mononymous.

I remember, in my childhood, I had this great nationalistic feeling for mononyms, but I did not have a name for it back then. So finding out about this word, mononymous, on the web, was a blast for me. There are people who are also mononymous, and I vaguely remember searching out popular people in India, including celebrities, who are legally mononymous. One of the examples is Kajol, that was pretty interesting for me at that time.

There are various advantages to being mononymous. First of all, in an academic setting, like a school or college, an examiner or a person taking a viva or your oral examination cannot judge you by just your surname. I don’t have a surname legally, so they cannot have, you know, a casteist judging of me and give me (or not give me) preference based on that. Similarly, it works in jobs as well. You don’t offer people a thing to discriminate you from other people just by looking at your name. So, that is pretty awesome.

My name is also unique in itself. I have found people who have the name Hemish within India, but the count is very low. Even just by searching my first name, a lot of things about me show up on a web search. So yeah, I don’t require a last name for my name to be unique.

It works the same way for usernames. On a lot of websites, I get my username "hemish". On the websites where I do not get it, I just use "imhemish", where "im" stands for "I am".

This is also why I’m a believer that people should abolish last names. What purpose do last names provide other than just discrimination? One of the purposes is just to identify you from a pool of people who have the same name as you, that’s it really. I know that people would say, yeah, there are other purposes.

I had considered in my childhood to get a last name added to my documents, but that’s a lot of hassle. Every document I’ve possessed since childhood needs to be changed, and that’s a lot of hassle I don’t want to go through. And I like my name like this. So yeah, thans to my dad for giving me this banger name.

Pronunciation

My name "Hemish" is spoken like how you would speak it in Spanish (Spanish doesn't have differing pronunciations for vowels like English). Indic writings of my name are हेमिश and ਹੇਮਿਸ਼. Although interestingly, my birth certificate still names me as "हेमीश", but that is fine.

I’ve run into issues with it too, because a lot of people can't pronounce it. I’ve heard various variations, including Himesh, the most popular one, credit goes to Himesh Reshamiya. Then there is Hamish, and there is a “Himanish” I have heard. A lot of them exist, and I’m now used to not correcting people about my name. If people ask me how they should pronounce it, then I’m very happy to guide them through the pronunciation. But by default, I do not explain the pronunciation at all, and that is fine with me.

I’m not a big celebrity or a person to even guide people on how my name is spelled or pronounced. So I mean that people cannot pronounce my name; that’s a big feeling in itself. Those people are not worthy of pronouncing my name if they cannot.

So this was my name, and this forms my identity on the web also.

entry.title: Guide to Running Citrix Workspace on Ubuntu 26.04+
entry.content:
Background

Citrix Workspace is an app to access hosted VDI (Virtual Desktop Infrastructure), but it is notorious to setup on newer Linux distributions like Ubuntu 26.04.

Windows is not my primary workspace for personal use, and I have a hard time re-adjusting to even doing personal stuff on Windows because my workflow is highly linked to GNOME ecosystem and Linux in general. So, naturally had to figure out installing it on Linux.

I began with Citrix Download Page and was downloading a .deb package. Appeareantly, Citrix maintains two versions of Linux package: Tech Preview and normal prod. The normal one is compiled with gcc8 compatibility and uses a lot of older libraries. Tech Preview has gcc11 compatibility and uses (some, not all) newer libraries.

I started with the normal package, as it must be stable, which happens to be 2604.10 as of September, 2026. I installed it the regular way, by command line by using sudo apt install ./icaclient<version>.deb

The install went fine, but I was not able to launch the workspace app from the app menu of my desktop.

Warning

If you are following any steps, do it at your own discretion. I would not be responsible for any damages to your system, or any blocks.

Request

Even if you are referring to one part of this article, as there are multiple approaches enlisted in this article, please do read the entire article, as a lot of things are interlinked with each other, and the knowledge of other may help you to get a solution of some problem you might be facing, particularly the GDK_BACKEND environment variable to be set to x11.

Issues with current package on Ubuntu 26.04

The issues I disovered by reading many articles, forums on Internet and exploring around the package are:

  • The package is compatible with Ubuntu 22.04 and related distros, doesn't work well with packages of newer versions.
  • It uses a lot of older libraries, including libwebkit2gtk which is basically webview like thing for gtk2, which is long EOL and removed in newer distros.
  • A lot of libraries accompanying libwebkit2gtk including older libsoup, libxml2, etc. have the same fate.

No Support from Citrix

Linux support may vary between organizations. Check your organization's current guidance before relying on Linux access.

Citrix itself does not package Linux that thoroughly as mainstreams operating systems like Windows or macOS. The most it does is bare-bones packaging, and some documentation for some configurations.

So, Linux users are kinda on their own.

Xorg and Wayland situation

Citrix is compatible with xorg (x11) only, and does not support Wayland. Ubuntu 26.04 and distros released in contemporary time of Ubuntu 26.04 ship version of GNOME as 50 or later, which removed support for Xorg sessions. So, naturally Ubuntu 26.04 does not have an option to switch to "Ubuntu on Xorg" session on the login window (GDM). Citrix can run as a xwayland process (basically, Citrix will call standard Xorg APIs, a standalone X server runs inside your desktop environment, and the windows running inside Xorg, are displayed in your Wayland session. It works pretty seamless, except for some things.

While, it CAN RUN as xwayland process, it is not configured to do so by default in a Wayland-only environment. So, basically when you launch it inside a Wayland-only environment (like default Ubuntu 26.04 session), the gtk runs as wayland, and GDK_BACKEND running is x11 and not wayland.

This thing, I discovered when I was using the Tech preview package (gcc11 compatible), it worked fine with linking a missing library, in logs I saw issues about EGL buffers. Consider EGL buffers as an API for graphics in Wayland. So, the thing which was being used by Citrix does not support EGL Buffers (and thus basically does not support Wayland). The best solution to this is to launch Citrix with GDK_BACKEND set to x11 as an environment variable, so it defaults to being an xwayland process. I will cover this solution later in the article.

Do note that the Ubuntu-based distros with environments other than GNOME may ship a Xorg session (like Cinnamon as on Linux Mint, XFCE as on LM XFCE & Xubuntu, etc.) In that case, you can just use the Xorg session of your desktop environment.

The Solutions

There are various possible solutions for successfully using Citrix on a newer Linux base like Ubuntu 26.04, all with their own caveats and benefits.

The Symbolic Library Linking (not recommended)

So, basically, as we discussed, Citrix is compiled against older versions of certain libraries. For example, if you launch Citrix Workspace via command line binary selfservice present in /opt/Citrix/ICAClient and see the logs, it might say libxml2.so.2: cannot open shared object file. This happens because the newer versions of this library would provide newer .so files like libxml2.so.16 which are not binary compatible with the older ABI.

Some people, including me, tried to create a symlink from libxml2.so.2 to libxml2.so.16, but as we said it is not binary compatible exactly, and certain functionality might break. I was able to launch the newer Tech preview (gcc11 build) of Citrix with this way, but this is not the recommended method and I would thus not cover the steps how to do it.

Using a Container (like Distrobox or your own managed Podman/Docker)

Distrobox is a tool, which can run other distributions (including their own versions) inside a container in your own operating system. The difference from standard Podman/Docker is that it provides multiple helpers and default configurations that allow the applications inside the containers to behave like they are running natively in your host OS, including features like, but not limited to, linking your home directory in container and host OS, wayland and xorg integrations, exporting .desktop files so that they appear in your app menu, etc. The benefit of this approach is you can use an older version of distros which has older libraries required for some particular software, and this will not pollute your host OS's libraries.

Please refer the two options you have:

Install the stuff yourself

Here is a guide which describes installing Citrix in a Distrobox container and exporting it to the host desktop:

  1. Install Podman and Distrobox on the host. For Fedora, run sudo dnf install podman distrobox; on Ubuntu, install Podman with sudo apt update followed by sudo apt install podman -y, then install Distrobox using the method recommended for your distribution.
  2. Create and enter a container based on a distribution with the required libraries, such as Ubuntu 22.04 or Fedora 42:
distrobox create --name citrix-env --image ubuntu:22.04
distrobox enter citrix-env

Fedora users can instead create a Fedora 42 container with distrobox create --name citrix-env --image registry.fedoraproject.org/fedora:42.

  1. Download the Citrix package for the container's distribution to ~/Downloads. In a Fedora container, install webkit2gtk3 and the RPM package with sudo dnf install webkit2gtk3 and sudo dnf install ~/Downloads/ICAClient*.rpm. In an Ubuntu container, run sudo apt update, install libwebkit2gtk-4.0.37, and install the downloaded package with sudo apt install ./Downloads/icaclient_*.deb.
  2. Export the application to the host menu with distrobox-export --app icaclient. If that application name is not found, try selfservice, wfica, or Citrix. You can also locate the .desktop file with find /usr/share/applications /opt/Citrix -name "*.desktop" and export that file directly.
  3. If the app starts with the wrong display backend, set GDK_BACKEND=x11 for the selfservice process, as described earlier.

Another article is available on GitHub Gist at Citrix Workspace on Linux (Distrobox + Ubuntu 24.04 + DistroShelf)

The better way: a pre-packaged script for you to set Distrobox with Citrix

An install and uninstall script can set up the container, export the apps, and help update the installation. The publicly available project and its instructions are in trapexit/distrobox-citrix.

Satisfying the required older dependencies directly inside your host OS

This approach is the one I'm following on my own system. While containers are generally light, as they share the same kernel as host OS, they still introduce some memory overhead (which is quite essential these days). So, I try to keep my installation light, with no containers.

What this approach does is, it basically downloads the older dependencies against which Citrix is compiled, from external sources (as they have been removed from repos of Ubuntu 26.04 or related distros), and puts them in a way so that Citrix can find them. Again, there can be 2 approaches here:

Installing the packages of older libraries

Various people prefer this method, as it is easier to download .deb packages of required dependencies, and just install them via apt or dpkg and they are automatically available in the LD path and thus directly accessible by selfservice binary.

For the libwebkit2gtk issue, the concise fix is to download compatible Ubuntu 22.04 packages for libicu70, libjavascriptcoregtk-4.0-18, and libwebkit2gtk-4.0-37, then install them in dependency order. For example:

wget http://archive.ubuntu.com/ubuntu/pool/main/i/icu/libicu70_70.1-2_amd64.deb
wget http://archive.ubuntu.com/ubuntu/pool/main/w/webkit2gtk/libjavascriptcoregtk-4.0-18_2.48.5-0ubuntu0.22.04.1_amd64.deb
wget http://archive.ubuntu.com/ubuntu/pool/main/w/webkit2gtk/libwebkit2gtk-4.0-37_2.48.5-0ubuntu0.22.04.1_amd64.deb

sudo apt install ./libicu70_70.1-2_amd64.deb
sudo apt install ./libjavascriptcoregtk-4.0-18_2.48.5-0ubuntu0.22.04.1_amd64.deb
sudo apt install ./libwebkit2gtk-4.0-37_2.48.5-0ubuntu0.22.04.1_amd64.deb

An alternative set of package versions is to download these packages from the public Ubuntu mirrors:

wget http://mirrors.edge.kernel.org/ubuntu/pool/main/w/webkit2gtk/libwebkit2gtk-4.0-37_2.48.3-0ubuntu0.22.04.1_amd64.deb
wget http://mirrors.edge.kernel.org/ubuntu/pool/main/i/icu/libicu70_70.1-2_amd64.deb
wget http://mirrors.edge.kernel.org/ubuntu/pool/main/w/webkit2gtk/libjavascriptcoregtk-4.0-18_2.48.3-0ubuntu0.22.04.1_amd64.deb

Then install the package set together with sudo dpkg -i ~/Downloads/lib*.deb after ensuring the download directory contains only the intended packages.

This approach avoids adding older Ubuntu repositories to a newer installation, which can cause repository conflicts. Install only the specific compatible packages you need. Package versions and mirrors may change or become unavailable over time. These dependency fixes do not address the GDK_BACKEND=x11 issue in Wayland-only sessions, so apply that separately if needed.

Extracting older libraries into a local path, and adding them to LD path

This is the sub-method that I prefer, though you are free to follow the previous sub-method as well. I like this method, because it does not pollute my package list, with these packages (though you might have a different opinion). Keeping the older libraries in a private compatibility directory avoids interfering with Ubuntu's system libraries.

A great person has put a guide on this, which is available at Citrix Workspace Ubuntu 26 Installation and Troubleshoot. This person, is also on Ubuntu 26.04, so this guide is the most compatible with newer Ubuntu versions. The article is itself an interesting read, as he describes how he got to know what older libraries he has to actually install by using standard linux ld tools to find out that header files are required.

What he does is basically downloads the older libraries, extracts them a separate dedicated folder named citrix-compat and puts that as a discoverable path to the citrix binary by running the binary with an environment variable.

Notes and additions to the above article

There are some additions I would like to add to this article:

Cleaner directory name

The original article uses:

~/citrix-compat

This creates a visible directory directly inside your home directory.

A cleaner alternative is:

~/.citrix-compat

Another option is:

~/.local/share/citrix-compat

If you use a different directory, change the path everywhere it appears, including:

  • The mkdir command
  • The dpkg-deb -x commands
  • The find commands
  • The LD_LIBRARY_PATH commands
  • The launcher script
X11 backend option

On systems using Wayland, Citrix may work more reliably when forced to use the X11 backend.

Add this near the top of the launcher script:

export GDK_BACKEND=x11

The complete launcher script can be:

#!/bin/bash

export GDK_BACKEND=x11

COMPAT_DIR="$HOME/citrix-compat" # Change this to actual directory name you use

export LD_LIBRARY_PATH="$COMPAT_DIR/usr/lib/x86_64-linux-gnu:$LD_LIBRARY_PATH"

exec /opt/Citrix/ICAClient/selfservice "$@"
Citrix app protection

When installing .deb file, you may be prompted to ask if you want to install Citrix app protection, and another thing as well. Please click yes/allow in each of it, because your organisation might require Citrix app protection to access its systems.

Creating a .desktop file for the same

It may be cumbersome to launch the launcher script in terminal every time, so duplicate the already existing Citrix Workspace .desktop file present in /usr/share/applications/ by copying it to ~/.local/share/applications/citrox-compat.desktop. Change the Exec and TryExec properties to the point to the the script you created, in this article /usr/local/bin/citrix-workspace. Also, change the name in Name field to differentiate it from original Citrix Workspace menu entry, for example I named it "Citrix Compat".

So, in essence, my ~/.local/share/applications/citrox-compat.desktop looks like:

[Desktop Entry]
Type=Application
Name=Citrix Compat
Comment=Citrix Workspace app for remote desktop access
Exec=/usr/local/bin/citrix-workspace
Icon=citrix-workspace
Categories=Network;RemoteAccess;
StartupNotify=true
Terminal=false

Peace out ☮️

entry.title: Helped a Homie with BITSCTF Using Python Internals
entry.content:
A random Sunday at home, I get a call from my friend skye (asli naam nhi likhne de rha (he is not letting me write his original name)). He was, as usual, fiddling with cybersec stuff, sparing time from his busy gaming schedule. Initially, I ignored the call, but then answered. He was participating in BITSCTF '25. He quickly asks me to have a look at a python file he sent me.

I, excited, opened the file, and I see the following Python one-liner:

# Python obfuscation by freecodingtools.org
                    
_ = lambda __ : __import__('zlib').decompress(__import__('base64').b64decode(__[::-1]));exec((_)(b'==QfWoizP8/vvPv/tu.........a lot of random stuff...........WiUxyW7lVwJe'))

aahhhhh... so much random characters

The goal was to find a flag.

Let's first understand what the code is doing:

  • First, a lambda function is being used. A lambda function allows definition of a function in a single line. It takes an argument (here __). It is followed by : which defines what the function should return. The function is assigned into a variable _.

  • __import__('zlib').decompress(...) is equivalent to the following, thanks to Python's metaprogramming functions:

import zlib
zlib.decompress(...)
  • Similarly, __import__('base64').b64decode(...) is equivalent to the following:
import base64
base64.decode(...)

  • __[::-1]), as everyone knows, reverses the string __ (which is the argument for the function).

  • ;: A lot of people don't know, but Python supports semicolons. It, like in any other languages, can be used to separate two statements. It's not necessary, and also not a standard, but is useful to make one-liners (as here two python statements are there in a single line)

  • exec(...): It treats strings as Python statements, for example exec("print('Hello World')") would treat the string as a Python statement and execute it, resulting in output Hello World.

  • The random string which is given is actually encoded string, given as a raw binary string (base64 takes binary strings by default). The _ function is thus called on the random string, passing the random string as the argument __.

In essence, the function first reverses the string passed to it, decodes it via base64, and then decompresses it via zlib. This is called on the random string.

I was feeling sus(picious) about the code as it is random string, and upon decoding, it could be any malicious code, and it is being run by exec. But, I took the riks, and executed the code. What output do I get?

Hello, World!

Looks like a normal "Hello World!", huh

I replaced the exec with a print to see what code is being executed, instead of seeing the "Hello World!" output of the code:

# Python obfuscation by freecodingtools.org
                    
_ = lambda __ : __import__('zlib').decompress(__import__('base64').b64decode(__[::-1]));print((_)(b'==QfWoizP8/vvPv/tu.......................a lot of random stuff............................WiUxyW7lVwJe'))

Running this, I get the output:

b"exec((_)(b'=cE3wh5B//7.....a lot of random stuff..............xyWzlNwJe'))"

W-w-whaaaatttt? The output is also a new python code using that function. I can't just exec it again. I need to find the stuff encoded in it. So, I strip out the b"exec( at start and )" at the end, to retrieve the contained string, and not execute it. I add the print statement to display it. In essence, I executed this:

_ = lambda __ : __import__('zlib').decompress(__import__('base64').b64decode(__[::-1]));
print((_)(b'=cE3wh5B.........a lot of random stuff.....yWzlNwJe'))

The string passed in this is not the string given initially. This string is the one generated by the run of program.

Executing the above code, I get the output:

b"exec((_)(b'==AiELbHP4///....a lot of random stuff......Bt7jfZBVgcxyW0lVwJe'))"

aaaahhhhh.... another one

How long should this go? I visited the website given in comment in the initial program: freecodingtools.org. From the homepage, I found "Python Obfuscator", which says:

Python code is ran through this algorithm 100s of times, each time making it more secure and unreadable.

100s? aah. I wrote a for loop to automate this decoding the string.

But where to break the loop? The loop should break when the decoding is no longer possible, i.e. an exception is raised by any of the decoding functions base64decode or zlib.decompress

This is the loop I wrote:

decode_obfuscated = lambda __ : __import__('zlib').decompress(__import__('base64').b64decode(__[::-1]))
string = '==AiELbHP4///....a lot of random stuff......Bt7jfZBVgcxyW0lVwJe'

for i in range(100):
    try:
        temp = decode_obfuscated(string)
        string = temp[11:-3]
        
    except:
        print(temp)
        print(string)
        break
  • The string slicing [11:-3] strips out b"exec((_)(b' from start and '))" from end, to get the string of new iteration.
  • When the decompression or decoding is no longer possible, exception is raised and loop is terminated via 'break' statement.

Running the program:

b'# Online Python Compiler\n\nprint("Hello, World!")\n# BITSCTF{obfuscation_and_then_some_more_obfuscation_4a4a4a4a}'
b'thon Compiler\n\nprint("Hello, World!")\n# BITSCTF{obfuscation_and_then_some_more_obfuscation_4a4a4a'

Flag found:

obfuscation_and_then_some_more_obfuscation_4a4a4a4a, bye

entry.title: Building SmartCam
entry.content:
What are we going to build?

We are going to build a sample page of an app in flutter, which captures the image from camera, and then displays the description of the image, and also speaks it through description. The description is fetched through Gemini API.

Prerequisites

  • A system with minimum 8 gb of ram
  • Flutter installed and configured on the system
  • Flutter extension installed in VS Code

Creating new project

Visual Studio Code and other IDE's provide us with ways to automatically create new flutter project with boiler plate code already written, along with all the build files.

In VS Code, press Ctrl+Shift+P and type 'Flutter'. You would see Flutter: New Projectoption. Click on the option, and you would be asked to select the folder you want to create project in. After selecting the folder, select 'New Application'. Enter the name of the project, and the project structure would be created.

Understanding directory structure

Flutter follows a defined directory structure for the projects.

Here are the most important sub-directories:

android, ios, linux, macos, web, windows

These hold platform-specific build files to run the project on these platforms

lib

The cross-platform code we write for the app

pubspec.yaml

Holds the package information

Removing the unncessary boilerplate

By default, Flutter provides a counter app. First, remove the MyHomePage from main.dart and unncessary comments. You can also remove the color theme if you want.

Installing the required packages

We are going to require these packages for various functionalities:

camera

Provides access to cameras on multiple platforms

flutter_tts

Provides Google's Text To Speech Services on various platforms

flutter_gemini

Provides access to Gemini inside a Flutter app

You can install these packages by running these commands in the terminal:

flutter pub add camera flutter_tts flutter_gemini

Creating the SmartCam screen

Create a new file in lib directory. Give it a suitable name, say smart_cam.dart.

We need to import Flutter's material library to use widgets. We also need flutter_gemini and flutter_ttsfor the respective functionalities.

import 'package:flutter/material.dart';
import 'package:flutter_gemini/flutter_gemini.dart';
import 'package:flutter_tts/flutter_tts.dart';

SmartCam(this.language);

Building the UI

From this onwards, all of the code needs to be run on system, and can not run on DartPad.

Initialising the camera

camera package provides the camera functionality. According to the documentation, we will create two variables in the state:

  • late List<CameraDescription> _cameras;- Holds the list of cameras available on the system. It would be initialised late when the state is initialised.
  • CameraController? controller;- Holds the CameraController for the current camera. It provides the methods to read camera feed. It can be null because certain systems may not have any camera.

Now, we will create an void initState() method according to the documentation:

@override
  void initState() {
    super.initState();
    availableCameras().then((value) {
      _cameras = value;
      controller = CameraController(_cameras[0], ResolutionPreset.max);
      controller?.initialize().then((_) {
        if (!mounted) {
          return;
        }
        setState(() {});
      }).catchError((Object e) {
      });
    });
  }

Displaying the camera feed

Now, we would first understand some other variables required in the state.

Put these variables in the state:

bool processing = false;
Uint8List? image;
String description = '';
  • processing - It indicates whether the image captured has finished processing
  • image - It stores the captured image.
  • description - It holds the textual description of image showed in UI in the bottom.

Now, we need to display the camera feed into the UI we created. We had put a placeholder for showing the camera feed. We will replace that with a Stack widget because Stack can hold multiple widgets in it.

Create a method _showImage which will return the widgets in stack:

List<Widget> _showImage(CameraController? controller, Uint8List? image) {
    if (controller == null) {
      return <Widget>[
        SizedBox(
          width: 1,
        )
      ];
    } else if (processing == false) {
      return <Widget>[
        CameraPreview(controller),
      ];
    } else if (processing == true) {
      return <Widget>[
        Image.memory(image!),
        Positioned.fill(
            child: Center(child: CircularProgressIndicator.adaptive()))
      ];
    } else {
      return <Widget>[
        CameraPreview(controller),
      ];
    }
  }
  • If the camera is not initialised, i.e. controller is null, then show nothing. For it, we have placed a SizedBox with nothing in it.
  • If the image is processing, show that static image on screen and do not show the camera feed. Since, image variables stores the captured image in memory, we use Image.network to display that image. Positioned.fill along with Center widget with CircularProgressIndicator, displays a loading circular indicator above captured image.
  • If the there is no image being processed, show the camera feed and not static image via use of CameraPreview.

Inside the build method of state, use description inside Text widget, like:

Text(description,
    style: TextStyle(color: Colors.white
)

Integrating Gemini

To integrate Gemini, we first need to import and initialise Gemini package (which we already installed) in the main.dart file. Put this code inside main.dart inside the void main() function, before the runApp(const MyApp()); statement.

WidgetsFlutterBinding.ensureInitialized();
Gemini.init(apiKey: 'your key here');

You need to get this key from https://aistudio.google.com/app/apikey.

Now, in smart_cam.dart file, create a variable inside state:

final gemini = Gemini.instance;

Now, create a method:

void _describeImage() async {
    var picture = await controller?.takePicture();
    var b = await picture?.readAsBytes();
    setState(() {
      processing = true;
      image = b;
    });
    var response = await gemini.textAndImage(
        text:
            "What does this show? Respond in ${widget.language} language with 3-4 lines",
        images: [b!]);
    var p = response?.outputPart as TextPart;
    setState(() {
      description = p.text;
      processing = false;
    });
    tts.speak(p.text);
}

This method captures the picture from CameraController, reads it as bytes, and then sets processing to true, and sets the captured image. This ensures UI is built again to reflect that image is captured and is being processed, i.e. a static captured image would be shown, along with circular progress indicator above it.

Then, it sends the image to Gemini along with the prompt, and receives the text from it, and then sets description to the text received from Gemini and sets processing to false again. This ensures description is now shown in the UI and the static image is again replaced by camera feed.

Integrating TextToSpeech

In smart_cam.dart file, import the package for TextToSpeech:

import 'package:flutter_tts/flutter_tts.dart';

In the SmartCamState, create a variable:

final tts = FlutterTts();

Inside initState method, add the following:

if (widget.language.toLowerCase() == 'hindi') {
      tts.setLanguage('hi');
}

It ensures that if language is Hindi, correct language is chosen for TextToSpeech.

In the _describeImage method, add the following at the end:

tts.speak(p.text);

This ensures the text which is received from Gemini is spoken by TextToSpeech.

Conclusion

So, we just built a simple flutter project including the vision capabilities of Gemini with camera.

The full code at the end looks like this:

import 'package:flutter_gemini/flutter_gemini.dart';
import './smart_cam.dart';

void main() {
  WidgetsFlutterBinding.ensureInitialized();
  Gemini.init(apiKey: 'your key here');
  runApp(const MyApp());
}

class MyApp extends StatelessWidget {
  const MyApp({super.key});

  @override
  Widget build(BuildContext context) {
    return MaterialApp(
      debugShowCheckedModeBanner: false,
      title: 'Flutter Demo',
      home: SmartCam('hindi'),
    );
  }
}

smart_cam.dart

import 'dart:typed_data';
import 'package:camera/camera.dart';
import 'package:flutter/material.dart';
import 'package:flutter_gemini/flutter_gemini.dart';
import 'package:flutter_tts/flutter_tts.dart';

class SmartCam extends StatefulWidget {
  final String language;
  SmartCam(this.language);

  @override
  State<SmartCam> createState() => _SmartCamState();
}

class _SmartCamState extends State<SmartCam> {
  late List<CameraDescription> _cameras;
  CameraController? controller;

  bool processing = false;
  Uint8List? image;
  String description = '';

  final gemini = Gemini.instance;
  
  final tts = FlutterTts();

  @override
  void initState() {
    super.initState();
    if (widget.language.toLowerCase() == 'hindi') {
      tts.setLanguage('hi');
    }
    availableCameras().then((value) {
      _cameras = value;
      controller = CameraController(_cameras[0], ResolutionPreset.max);
      controller?.initialize().then((_) {
        if (!mounted) {
          return;
        }
        setState(() {});
      }).catchError((Object e) {
      });
    });
  }

  List<Widget> _showImage(CameraController? controller, Uint8List? image) {
    if (controller == null) {
      return <Widget>[
        SizedBox(
          width: 1,
        )
      ];
    } else if (processing == false) {
      return <Widget>[
        CameraPreview(controller),
      ];
    } else if (processing == true) {
      return <Widget>[
        Image.memory(image!),
        Positioned.fill(
            child: Center(child: CircularProgressIndicator.adaptive()))
      ];
    } else {
      return <Widget>[
        CameraPreview(controller),
      ];
    }
  }

  void _describeImage() async {
    var picture = await controller?.takePicture();
    var b = await picture?.readAsBytes();
    setState(() {
      processing = true;
      image = b;
    });
    var response = await gemini.textAndImage(
        text:
            "What does this show? Respond in ${widget.language} language with 3-4 lines",
        images: [b!]);
    var p = response?.outputPart as TextPart;
    setState(() {
      description = p.text;
      processing = false;
    });
    tts.speak(p.text);
  }

  @override
  void dispose() {
    controller?.dispose();
    super.dispose();
  }

  @override
  Widget build(BuildContext context) {
    return Scaffold(
        appBar: AppBar(
          title: Text("SmartCam"),
          backgroundColor: Colors.black54,
          foregroundColor: Colors.white,
        ),
        body: Center(
          child: GestureDetector(
            onLongPress: () {
              _describeImage();
            },
            child: Column(
                crossAxisAlignment: CrossAxisAlignment.center,
                children: [
                  Expanded(
                    child: Container(
                      color: Colors.black,
                      child: Container(
                          height:
                              2 * (MediaQuery.sizeOf(context).height / 3) - 60,
                          decoration: BoxDecoration(
                              border:
                                  Border.all(color: Colors.black, width: 13)),
                          child: Center(
                              child: ClipRRect(
                                  borderRadius: BorderRadius.circular(10),
                                  child: Stack(
                                      children:
                                          _showImage(controller, image))))),
                    ),
                  ),
                  Align(
                      alignment: Alignment.center,
                      child: Container(
                          width: MediaQuery.sizeOf(context).width,
                          color: Colors.black54,
                          child: Container(
                              padding: EdgeInsets.all(10),
                              margin: EdgeInsets.all(10),
                              decoration: BoxDecoration(
                                color: Colors.black54,
                                borderRadius: BorderRadius.circular(20),
                              ),
                              child: Text(
                                description,
                                style: TextStyle(color: Colors.white),
                              ))))
                ]),
          ),
        ));
  }
}

The code of this sits at GitHub repository: https://github.com/imhemish/smart_cam.
